title: The ultraviolet continuum slopes of galaxies at $\mathbf{z \gtrsim 12}$ selected from ${\mathbf{0.6 \, deg}^2}$ of JWST imaging
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, to be submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present an analysis of the ultraviolet (UV) continuum slopes $(β)$ of $55$ galaxies at $z\gtrsim 12$, selected from a wide-area ($>0.6$ sq. deg) search across publicly available JWST/NIRCam imaging. Our sample spans the absolute UV magnitude ($M_{\mathrm{UV}}$) range $-21.6 \leq M_{\mathrm{UV}} \leq -17.3$ and we find an inverse variance-weighted mean $\langleβ\rangle = -2.57\pm0.04$ indicating that, on average, the galaxy population is extremely blue at $z\gtrsim 12$. The average $β$ at these redshifts is consistent with the intrinsic stellar plus nebular continuum limit in the absence of UV dust-attenuation. Consistent with earlier JWST works, our analysis suggests that the moderately dust-attenuated galaxies at $z \lesssim 10$ become essentially attenuation-free by $z \simeq 11$. We find no evidence for a $β-M_{\mathrm{UV}}$ relation in our $z\gtrsim 12$ sample, indicating that the attenuation-free interpretation applies across all observed UV magnitudes. By augmenting our sample with previous JWST constraints down to $z=9$, and incorporating $M_{\mathrm{UV}}$-matched HST studies down to $z=4$, we find a smooth evolution in $β(z)$ over a wide range in redshift. The average value of $β$ becomes progressively bluer at $z>4$, with $\mathrm{d}β/\mathrm{d}z \simeq -0.1$. Finally, although we find that the typical galaxy at $z \gtrsim 12$ is consistent with the attenuation-free limit, the scatter in our individual $β$ measurements is consistent with the existence of a small population of dust-reddened galaxies with $β\gtrsim -2$.

title: Parallel alignment of radio AGN jets and large cosmic web structures in the direction of the Shapley supercluster
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 13 pages (+5 pages of appendix), 9 figures (+4 in appendix)
summary: Aims. We investigated the potential large-scale alignment of radio active galactic nuclei (AGN) jets in the proximity of the Shapley Supercluster (SSC) area and its correlation with the identified cosmic web structures. Methods. We analyzed 28 radio AGNs divided into two populations with comparable sky coverage north and south of a diffuse X-ray filamentary structure connecting clusters in the SSC core. We measured the average jet position angles (PAs) and combined them with spectroscopic redshifts to assess the persistence of the alignment along the line of sight. Results. We detected a significant large-scale alignment of the radio AGN jets with the foreground X-ray filament (oriented at PA $\sim$ 115$^\circ$ $\pm$ 10$^\circ$). Both the northern (PA $\sim$ 117$^\circ$) and southern (PA $\sim$ 129$^\circ$) groups align with this axis, yielding an overall statistical significance of 4.5 $σ$ (upper and lower bounds: 6.1$σ$, 3.8 $σ$). Although the projected alignment is highly significant, sparse spectroscopic coverage (seven sources spanning 0.048 $\lesssim$ z $\lesssim$ 0.55) suggests that this spatial coherence may extend beyond the SSC (z $\sim$ 0.048), hinting at a line-of-sight correlation across significantly larger cosmic scales. Conclusions. The observed alignment cannot be explained by localized dynamical processes alone. These findings may indicate a persistent influence of the large-scale structure of the cosmic web, or preferred directions of matter collapse, on supermassive black hole spin axes, highlighting a connection between AGN jet morphology and the underlying dark matter distribution. Such alignments represent an important systematic that must be accounted for in precision cosmology with surveys such as Euclid.

title: Radiative Transfer Modeling of Multi-Shell Molecular Outflows in the Class 0 Protostar IRAS 15398-3359
comment: 29 pages, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Recent high-angular-resolution observations of protostellar outflows have revealed complex spatial and velocity structures that are difficult to describe with a single shell. We have investigated the primary outflow of the Class 0 protostar IRAS 15398$-$3359 in the H$_2$CO and CS emission observed with ALMA and identified four shell-like components, which trace the cavity walls of the more extended CO outflows. Non-LTE radiative-transfer calculations of H$_2$CO and synthetic ALMA observations of the three-dimensional model show that a common ellipsoidal geometrical form and Hubble-law-like velocity field can broadly reproduce the channel-map and position--velocity structures of the identified shells when the geometry, spatial configuration, and kinematics of each shell are allowed to vary independently. The kinematic timescales and inclination angles of the inner and outer shells are $\sim$1000 yr ($19^\circ$ and $15^\circ$) and $\sim$750 yr ($5^\circ$ and $8^\circ$), respectively. The momentum injection rate of the outer bipolar pair is approximately 2.2 times that of the inner pair. The inferred $\dot{M}_{\rm wind}/\dot{M}_{\rm acc}$ ratios are $0.7$--$3\%$ and $2$--$7\%$ for the inner and outer shells. The observed shell-to-shell differences suggest episodicity of the mass ejection events, where the strength and direction of the outflow activity may vary over short timescales of order $10^2$--$10^3$ yr.

title: Active Learning for Molecular Discovery: A Retrospective Test toward TMC-1
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables; submitted to ApJ; code and data at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23312984
summary: Machine-learning recommendation lists can help prioritize searches for new interstellar molecules, but whether reranking such a list as detections accumulate improves on it has not been tested. We present a pre-registered retrospective test toward TMC-1, using a published machine-learning list of 1,510 recommended candidates, consolidated to 1,434 candidates, and the species reported there through September 2026. At four annual origins from 2022 to 2025, a logistic-regression ranking on seven released features, refit on the detections known at each origin, separates later detections from never-detected candidates with a pooled AUC of 0.867, against 0.706 for the best single-criterion baseline (difference 0.160; 95\% interval 0.095-0.230). The advantage persists under a shifted date boundary and two alternative feature regimes, but is not established among the top 100 candidates (12 versus 7 detections). A searcher that refits on its own observations reaches half of the 63 detected species on the list in a median of 200 observations, against 332 for the best fixed ordering and 717.5 expected for random search. Uncertainty sampling, the standard active-learning rule, performs worse than random (AUC 0.210): later detections lie at low predictive uncertainty, close to known chemistry. Of 101 species in our validation set, 37 are absent from the list, and only 13 of these appear in a pool rebuilt from its source databases, including 2 of 11 radicals and neither ion. Candidate generation, not ranking, is the main constraint. We release 100 recommended targets, with code and frozen inputs, for prospective testing.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): Spacecraft performance in the L2 environment
comment: 38 pages, 33 figures; companion paper of Euclid DR1
summary: The Euclid mission was designed around the need for thermo-optical and mechanical stability, stray-light suppression, low outgassing, and precise guiding. After three years in space, a wealth of data is available to assess the performance in these areas. We review the L2 halo-orbit design and consumables budget. Solar stray-light gradually increases by 14\% per year and is consistent with meteoroid puncturing, but remains low overall. Data loss from high solar activity has declined notably since the maximum of the 25th Solar cycle passed. The thermodynamical response of the optical elements to a thermal step impulse follows sigmoidal growth curves, entering the asymptotic equilibration regime after 21--46 hours. Water-ice contamination has affected data from both instruments and requires continued monitoring; we review detection and decontamination methods, and Euclid's contamination history. High-precision measurements of the zodiacal background reveal, at eight sigma significance, the subtle modulation caused by the changing perspective on the dust distribution due to the L2 halo-orbit libration. These data also show that conservative pre-launch estimates overestimated the out-of-field stray-light by factors of 4 (H band) to 27 (I band). Telemetry data demonstrate excellent guiding, and enable highly significant detections of solar radiation pressure and of thermal-emission recoil from Euclid's unilluminated dark sides. Lastly, we present a list of 34 meteoroid impacts, discuss their mechanical and optical signatures, and derive a minimum detectable impactor mass of 5e-7 g.

title: Mass Loss Rates of Evolved Stars in Isolated Dwarf Galaxies
summary: We derive the mass-loss rates of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars in the isolated dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 6822 using SEDust, an automated pipeline that fits spectral energy distributions (SEDs) to estimate stellar mass-loss and dust-production rates. The total mass-loss rate of the AGB population is $(3.7 \pm 1.1) \times 10^{-3} M_\odot\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. For a gas-to-dust ratio of 200, this corresponds to a dust injection rate of $2.0 \times 10^{-5} M_\odot\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. If sustained over 10 Gyr, this rate would yield approximately $2 \times 10^{5} M_\odot$ of dust, which is lower than the dust mass of $2.7 \times 10^{5} M_\odot$ estimated from Herschel observations. AGB stars alone therefore cannot account for the present-day dust reservoir of NGC 6822, and additional sources or processes, such as dust growth in the interstellar medium, are required.

title: Sailing with the winds of HL Tau: the JWST view
comment: 20 pages, 16 figures, accepted by A&A
summary: Studying protostellar ejections is crucial to understanding the formation of young stars and planetary systems. The Class I/II star HL Tau, with its ringed disk and prominent bipolar outflows, is a benchmark system for these studies. We provide a first overview of our Cycle 3 JWST program targeting HL Tau, focusing on the morphology and kinematics of the various wind components as well as on the water emission lines excited in the inner disk. Our observations cover the 1.66-28 $μ$m spectral range, combining NIRSpec and MIRI MRS mosaics to map the inner 10" of the red-shifted lobe of the outflow and the base of the blue-shifted lobe. In the red-shifted lobe we observe a stratified wind of three nested layers: a fast, highly collimated atomic jet structured in a chain of eight knots and with radial velocities of 160 km/s; a wide-angle H$_2$ wind with velocities of 45 km/s exhibiting complex arc-like substructures; and a warm gas shell, of radial velocity of 35 km/s, visible in low-excitation transitions of CO ($ν$=1-0). This CO shell appears co-spatial with the CO (J=2-1) emission detected by ALMA with velocities from 3 to 25 km/s. In the first 1" of the blue-shifted lobe we detect a similar stratification, but the jet is faster and less collimated. The observed stratification and kinematics of the flow may support a magnetically driven disk-wind scenario in which the distinct components originate in the disk at progressively larger distances from the star. However, while the external components observed in CO have the laminar and regular appearance predicted for such winds, the knots in the inner jet and the arcs in the wind could be the manifestation of a pulsed ejection mechanism. Additionally, in MIRI spectra taken at the star position we detect a forest of water lines dominated by cold-to-warm (< 500 K) gas. Their distribution suggests an extended reservoir of sublimated ices.

title: Cosmic Ray Heating of the Early IGM: Realistic Galaxy Populations, Reduced Efficiency, and 21-cm Signatures
comment: 33 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to JCAP
summary: Cosmic rays (CRs) accelerated by the first supernovae could heat the intergalactic medium (IGM) before reionization. Previous 21-cm simulations, assuming a kinetic-energy power-law spectrum and simplified galaxy populations, found that CR heating can rival X-ray heating from high-mass X-ray binaries, imprint a distinct signature on the 21-cm power spectrum, and flatten the absorption trough of the global 21-cm signal. Here we model CR heating in 21cmFAST with: (i) the momentum power-law spectrum predicted by diffusive shock acceleration; (ii) Coulomb losses off free electrons; and (iii) injection from data-informed populations of atomic-cooling and molecularly cooled galaxies. We find that CR heating is about an order of magnitude weaker than previously estimated because a momentum power law places little energy in the sub-relativistic protons ($\lesssim 40$ MeV) that supply 99% of the heat. For our fiducial spectral slope, at the hard end of those inferred for Galactic supernova remnants, and for matched efficiency, this reduces the heating by a factor of $\approx 12$, and together with a more realistic galaxy model, by a factor of $\approx 28$ at $z = 15$. At the efficiencies that supernovae can supply, CR heating is weaker than standard X-ray heating, and the global signal alone cannot tell the two apart. Distinguishing CR from X-ray heating with the 21-cm power spectrum requires CR efficiencies a few times higher than those expected from local observations. At such efficiencies, CR heating yields up to $\approx 55\%$ more power than X-ray heating at matched global signal (median over scales), compared with only 3-6% at a locally motivated efficiency. A flattened absorption trough, like the one claimed by EDGES, requires efficiencies over two orders of magnitude above the local ones, beyond plausible Population III supernova budgets.

title: The Dark Side of the Periodic Table: Theory and Signatures of Nuclear Atomic Dark Matter
comment: 83 + 16 pages + Refs., 19 Figures, 4+2 Tables
summary: We study the theory and signatures of a Mirror Twin Higgs (MTH) scenario in which stable twin neutrons constitute most of the dark matter (DM), while a subdominant component of twin elements survives as nuclear atomic dark matter (naDM). This framework offers a solution to the $matter~coincidence~problem$ ($Ω_{\rm DM}\simeq5Ω_b$), as the twin $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry can correlate the visible and DM mass scales and their number densities. We analyze twin nucleon freeze-out and the onset of twin Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) to estimate the total naDM abundance, and determine which elements in the dark periodic table could be populated. An appreciable but subdominant naDM component generally requires a fractional nucleon mass splitting near the percent level, with twin-BBN creating heavy elements up to twin carbon. Strong twin neutron-proton scattering allows nearly all of the dark matter, not only the atomic sub-component, to participate in $dark~acoustic~oscillations$ (DAO) at early times, giving rise to a characteristic two-stage DAO signature that may be detected with future cosmological probes. Interactions between the twin and visible sectors, including the irreducible Higgs portal, make this scenario a well-motivated target for future directional direct-detection searches, and the naDM sub-component is expected to exhibit highly exotic astrophysics. We outline a supersymmetric twin Froggatt-Nielsen realization in which spontaneous $\mathbb{Z}_2$ breaking in the flavon sector can generate the required fermion spectrum and Higgs potential.

title: A giant dark matter core extending far beyond the stars of a dwarf galaxy
comment: 25 pages,17 figures, 5 tables, submitted to Nature Communications
summary: In the standard cosmological model, the distribution of cold dark matter (CDM) can be reshaped by baryonic processes through gravity, as gas outflows alter the central potential and transform steep cusps into nearly constant-density cores. However, such feedback-generated cores are generally expected to have sizes comparable to the visible stellar body of a galaxy. Here we report the discovery of an exceptionally extended dark matter core in a nearby gas-rich dwarf galaxy UGCA 320. We combine high-resolution MUSE H$α$ kinematics in the inner region with high-, medium-, and low-resolution MeerKAT HI observations from the MHONGOOSE survey tracing the galaxy out to large radii. After accounting for an additional non-circular kinematic component identified in the central HI spectra, we construct an extended rotation curve to constrain the dark matter distribution. The resulting rotation curve is poorly reproduced by a cuspy Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) halo but well described by cored pseudo-isothermal (ISO) and Burkert halo models. Consistently, a fit with a generalized NFW model yields an inner density slope of $γ=0.36\pm0.12$, quantitatively supporting a shallow central density profile. The best-fit ISO model gives a dark matter core radius of $7.62\pm0.80$ kpc, approximately four times the stellar half-light radius and substantially larger than typically found in dwarf galaxies. We investigate the main systematic uncertainties and find that the resulting core radii remain large, all lying within 3$σ$ of the fiducial fit. The exceptionally large core in UGCA 320 may pose a challenge to the standard CDM paradigm. While its properties are broadly consistent with self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), they may be difficult to reconcile with warm and fuzzy dark matter models, as well as the stellar feedback-driven core formation scenario.

title: Constraining Dark Matter Gravitational Production with the 21cm Signal at the Cosmic Dawn
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures, 1 table
summary: The origin of dark matter is one of the major problems in modern cosmology. We can infer its existence from the gravitational potential wells around astrophysical objects, but there is no convincing explanation for what its nature and origin are. Moreover, experiments for direct detection, indirect detection, or particle production in accelerators have not shown, until now, any conclusive interaction between dark matter and particles in the standard model. This may imply that dark matter does not interact with ordinary matter and originates from pure gravitational interaction. In this manuscript, we investigate the possibility to constrain the gravitational production of dark matter from the 21cm brightness temperature at the cosmic dawn. Considering only the time when the absorption profile occurs, we can impose upper limits on the dark matter's mass. Future measurements have potential to extend current constraints and help understanding the nature of dark matter.

title: Discrete Supernovae and the Limits of Continuous Models in Low-Mass Dark Matter Halos
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures; To be submitted to The Open Journal of Astrophysics; comments and feedback welcome
summary: Many galaxy formation models represent supernova feedback by a continuous energy injection rate averaged over the stellar initial mass function (IMF). This approximation can fail in low-mass dark matter halos, where single, discrete supernovae can unbind more gas than the reservoir holds. We investigate this using a one-zone model that characterises continuous and discrete supernova feedback at redshifts $z\geq5$. Both feedback modes inject the same expected energy per unit stellar mass formed. In the discrete model, individual supernovae are resolved and energy is injected instantaneously; in the continuous model, supernovae are IMF-averaged and energy injection is spread over a finite time interval. Once stars form, a supernova can unbind 1.5-2.7 times the gas present. Continuous feedback begins removing gas after $\sim 4$ Myr, whereas the first discrete supernova occurs after $\sim 10$ Myr, which produces a stellar mass excess before feedback takes effect. The excess persists because the reservoir responds nonlinearly: an event removes at most the gas present, and star formation halts once it is empty. It depends strongly on halo mass: from 135 per cent at $10^7\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to 15 per cent at $10^8\, \rm{M}_\odot$, to negligible at $10^9\, \rm{M}_\odot$ by $z=5$. Fixing the number and timing of supernovae does not remove the stellar excess, which indicates that it is not caused by stochastic IMF sampling. Instead, it vanishes when the same energy is divided among more, smaller events. Matching the energy released per unit stellar mass therefore does not guarantee equivalent feedback in halos that retain gas until the first supernova.

title: Diffuse interstellar bands in nearby galaxies with MaNGA: environmental trends with metallicity, extinction, ionization, and star-forming activity
comment: 12 pages of main text and 17 pages of appendices; 8 main-text figures and 20 appendix figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) are absorption features of uncertain origin observed in the optical and near-infrared spectra of stars and galaxies. Although their correlation with dust extinction is well established, the physical conditions governing their strength across different interstellar medium (ISM) environments remain poorly understood. We investigate the environmental dependence of the DIB $\lambda5780$ using spatially resolved MaNGA spectroscopy for 837 nearby galaxies spanning a broad range of stellar masses, star-formation rates, and ISM properties. Stellar and nebular parameters are derived via spectral fitting, while DIB absorption is measured from high-signal-to-noise spatially binned residual spectra. We detect the DIB $\lambda5780$ in 159 galaxies and report the most distant spatially resolved DIB detection to date, at 232 Mpc. The DIB $\lambda5780$ equivalent width correlates positively with both stellar and gas-phase extinction. DIB $\lambda5780$ is preferentially detected in regions of high extinction, near- or super-solar metallicity ($12+\log({\rm O/H})\gtrsim8.5$), and moderate specific star-formation rates ($-10.5\lesssim\log({\rm sSFR}/{\rm yr}^{-1})\lesssim-9$). By contrast, it falls below our detection threshold in metal-poor or strongly ionized environments. It is rarely detected in regions with little or no recent star formation, with the few detections in such environments occurring primarily in regions driven by composite ionization. Our results indicate that DIB $\lambda5780$ is preferentially detected, within the sensitivity limits of the MaNGA data, in dust-rich, chemically evolved, and moderately ionized environments.

title: Enhancing Graviton--Photon Conversion through Galactic Magnetic Turbulence
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures + Supplemental Materials(6 pages, 3 figures)
summary: Plasma dispersion suppresses coherent graviton-photon conversion over astrophysical distances. We show that Galactic magnetic turbulence enables phase matching by compensating the plasma-induced mismatch, allowing matched magnetic modes to contribute coherently. In the long path limit, the ensemble-averaged conversion probability grows linearly with propagation distance in the phase matched regime and is governed by the projected magnetic power spectrum. Applied to photon background observations, this mechanism yields characteristic strain limits that are stronger than previous Galactic conversion bounds in the inertial range phase matching window, with improvements of up to two orders of magnitude.

title: Rapidly Spinning Primordial Black Holes from Confinement
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, including Supplemental Material. Companion video: https://youtu.be/lrX_yWl8s1Q
summary: Confinement can turn widely separated particles into rapidly spinning primordial black holes. A flux tube pulls a heavy quark--antiquark pair together, converting its stored energy into relativistic motion. The same mechanism is possible in the magnetic dual, where a Higgs phase confines magnetic flux into a string joining a monopole--antimonopole pair. As the particles approach, cosmological tides and string bends can deflect their motion and make them miss. These disturbances can originate during inflation or be generated later. Black-hole formation then requires rare close passages from a smooth, broad encounter distribution. The resulting natal spin density therefore rises linearly to extremality, with mean dimensionless spin two thirds. Numerical string evolutions recover this law. Pairs that miss can remain bound, radiate and later collapse into lighter, near-extremal holes, sourcing a stochastic gravitational-wave background. Although the abundance remains model dependent, confinement leaves a unique spin signature that gravitational-wave observations can test.

title: Revisiting the distance to 4U 1543-475 through X-ray dust-scattering rings
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We derived a geometrical distance of the black-hole X-ray binary 4U 1543-475 based on X-ray dust-scattering rings associated with its 1992 and 2002 outbursts. We analyzed archival ROSAT and XMM-Newton observations and identified an X-ray dust-scattering ring in each observation, produced by two different dust layers along the line of sight. By combining the angular radii of the rings with the independently determined distances of the scattering dust layers and the epochs of the corresponding outbursts, we derive a best-constrained distance to 4U 1543-475 of 4.6 $\pm$ 0.2 kpc. This value is substantially smaller than the distance of 7.5 kpc commonly adopted in the literature and has important implications for the inferred physical properties of the system. In particular, the revised distance favors the presence of a low-mass extended-horizontal-branch donor star over a main-sequence star, calling for a reassessment of the dynamical parameters of the binary and, consequently, of the black-hole mass. The smaller distance also affects the inferred properties of the relativistic jet and the estimate of black-hole spin derived from the spectral continuum-fitting.

title: Tracing Galactic Dust Reddening with Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon Emission: SPHEREx Observations of the North Ecliptic Pole
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We investigate the ability of SPHEREx observations of the $3.3$ $μ$m polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission feature to trace Galactic dust reddening. Applying a spectral template-based method to SPHEREx data, we measure the strength of the $3.3$ $μ$m PAH feature in each $6''.2$ pixel of a $22^{\circ}$ by $22^{\circ}$ region centered on the north ecliptic pole (NEP). We convert the PAH feature strength to reddening by applying a radiation field correction and a linear scale factor. The resulting $E(B-V)$ map is consistent with far-infrared, stellar, and HI-based reddening maps at arcminute scales, exhibiting a typical $E(B-V)$ difference of $\lesssim 7$ mmag. A galaxy count test finds that all reddening maps have a dispersion of $\approx11$ mmag in $E(B-V)$ relative to what would be needed to produce spatially uniform galaxy counts. While there is some evidence that reddening is overestimated by our map at high PAH abundances, this effect is smaller than the uncertainties on the applied radiation field corrections and limited to $\sim$10 mmag in the most extreme regions of the NEP. For a diffuse, high Galactic latitude region like the NEP and at the sensitivities of our validation metrics, the SPHEREx PAH-emission based reddening map matches the accuracy of existing reddening maps while being capable of accessing a higher angular resolution of $\sim6''$.

title: Dark matter alters dwarf galaxy sizes and morphologies
summary: Dwarf galaxies are the most dark-matter-dominated systems in the Universe, serving as unique laboratories for exploring the fundamental nature of the dark sector. Although the observed diversity in dwarf galaxy sizes and morphologies suggests an interplay between dark matter and baryonic physics, this relationship has remained largely unquantified in existing models. Here, we utilize a set of novel cosmological simulations with baryons to demonstrate how dark matter physics directly drives the structural evolution of these galaxies. By comparing the same systems across cold dark matter and varied self-interacting dark matter models, we find that the evolution of the central density of dark matter significantly impacts a galaxy's half-light radius, but the signal is dependent on morphology. This causal link establishes galaxy size as a direct signature of the underlying dark matter microphysics. Our findings provide a predictive framework for decoding dark matter particle properties from galactic shapes, offering a roadmap for upcoming wide-field surveys, such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, to probe the dark sector through the statistical analysis of galaxy populations.

title: ViViViT: a Video-to-Video Vision Transformer for Cosmological Lightcone Reconstruction
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, Accepted to the Sim2Science Workshop (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Moving along the line of sight of a cosmological lightcone also moves through cosmic time, as in a video of cosmic structure traced by an evolving observable. We recast the reconstruction of the underlying matter field from observed lightcones as a video-to-video translation task by introducing ViViViT, a vision transformer that factorizes attention across transverse frames and radial evolution. On reconstructed matter fields from 21cm neutral hydrogen simulations over $z\in[7.66,16.00]$, ViViViT preserves spectral power and phase alignment within a few percent of the ground truth up to the Nyquist scale, and three-point correlations for all triangle configurations with sides up to $k\simeq0.77\,h/\mathrm{Mpc}$, outperforming a convolutional 3D-U-Net baseline across all measured statistics. By encoding the evolving geometry of the cosmological observable itself, ViViViT marks a step toward field-level architectures that natively respect cosmic time, opening the path to time-aware reconstruction of cosmic tracers and targeted searches for redshift-dependent signatures in 21cm data.

title: The origin of Potassium in Galactic chemical evolution - The effect of C-O shell mergers in massive stars
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) of potassium (K) and of most other odd-Z elements remains poorly understood: models generally underproduce the observed [K/Fe] over a wide metallicity range, depending on the adopted massive star yields. A proposed site for efficient K nucleosynthesis is the merger between the oxygen and carbon shells (C-O shell merger) that can occur in massive stars a few hours before core collapse. Some GCE models with specific yield sets have been shown to reconcile predictions with observations. Here we re-analyse these yield sets to quantify the contribution of C-O shell mergers to K production and what the Galactic evolution of K implies about the occurrence of these events. We analyse 194 pre-supernova models from three independent yield sets, covering a wide range of initial masses, metallicities and rotational velocities, and including both single and binary-stripped stars. We identify the progenitors undergoing a C-O shell merger and compute GCE models with and without their contribution. In all three sets, the enhanced K production can be traced back to a small number of C-O merger progenitors, which eject up to ~10-50 times more K than non-merger progenitors of similar mass. Without them, no model reproduces the observations and [K/Fe] is sub-solar over most of the metallicity range. With them, [K/Fe] is enhanced only within the metallicity window where mergers occur in each grid. Binarity itself plays a minor role, as single stars alone produce similar amounts of K. Since the K synthesised in a C-O merger is essentially primary, the observed nearly linear increase of [K/H] with [Fe/H] can be reproduced only if C-O shell mergers occur with a similar frequency at all metallicities. K could therefore be used to infer the occurrence rate of C-O shell mergers in massive stars as a function of time.

title: The 21 cm-Lyman-$α$ forest cross-power spectrum with a minimal effective field theory
comment: 31 pages, 11 figures, 8 tables
summary: Intensity maps of the 21 cm line and the Lyman-$α$ (Ly$α$) forest trace the same cosmic volume at $2\lesssim z\lesssim 4$. Their cross-power spectrum is insensitive to foregrounds that do not correlate between the two probes and, together with the Ly$α$ auto-spectrum, separates the mean 21 cm brightness temperature from the neutral hydrogen (HI) bias. Effective field theory models of each tracer exist, but at one loop they carry tens of nuisance parameters. We test whether a minimal effective field theory (mEFT), consisting of the tree-level Kaiser model with leading-order counterterms and stochastic terms, previously validated for the Ly$α$ auto-spectrum, describes the 21 cm auto-, Ly$α$ auto- and cross-power spectra jointly. We use the Sherwood 80 $h^{-1}$Mpc hydrodynamical simulation with HI painted onto halos at $z=2.4$-$4.2$, and reduce sample variance with Zel'dovich control variates. Each spectrum is validated separately and then in a joint fit with shared parameters. With scale cuts $k_{\rm max}=0.5$, $1.2$ and $2.0\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ for the 21 cm auto-, cross- and Ly$α$ auto-spectra, the mEFT fits all three spectra at all five redshifts. In the joint fit the mEFT determines the HI bias to 2.0-2.5% and the Ly$α$ density bias to 2.1-2.3%. The scale cuts follow the HI velocity dispersion and the Ly$α$ pressure-smoothing scale. When the brightness temperature is left free, the fits that include the cross-spectrum prefer values 20-30% above the true one, at 1-2$σ$, while the two auto-spectra together do not constrain it. A prior on the HI bias recovers the true value of the brightness temperature.

title: Bidimensional Exploration of the warm-Temperature Ionised gaS (BETIS) III. The impact of eDIG on strong-line abundance determinations in galactic halos
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Submitted to A&A
summary: The extraplanar diffuse ionised gas (eDIG) is a key tracer of the feedback processes that connect galactic discs and halos. We present the first study of spatially resolved gas-phase chemical abundances in the eDIG of edge-on galaxies, based on integral field spectroscopy obtained with MUSE. Using a sample of four galaxies from the BETIS sample, we derived maps of the oxygen abundance, 12+log(O/H), the nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio, log(N/O), and the ionisation parameter, log(U), with the HII-CHI-Mistry v5.5 code, and we tested the reliability of this method when different ionisation sources are present. We separated the eDIG into star-formation-dominated and shock-contaminated regimes according to the relative contribution of photoionisation and shocks, and investigated their impact on the derived chemical abundances. We find that HII-CHI-Mistry returns systematically lower O/H and N/O values in shock-contaminated regions, especially for N/O, with typical offsets of ~0.1-0.15 dex relative to star-formation-dominated regions, together with a more homogeneous and lower ionisation state (log(U) ~ -3.1). In contrast, star-formation-dominated regions span a wider range of ionisation parameters (log(U) ~ -3.3 to -2.8) while maintaining approximately solar oxygen abundances. Despite these differences, the abundance offsets are comparable to the sampling step of the HII-CHI-Mistry model grid. The inferred oxygen abundance shows little variation between discs and halos. This is compatible with a scenario in which star formation feedback and galactic fountains efficiently recycle oxygen-rich gas between both components, in agreement with hydrodynamical simulations. In contrast, the N/O ratio shows significant radial and vertical variations, particularly in environments with weaker star formation feedback.

title: The astrometric precision of incoherent pulsar timing arrays
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures
summary: We address the astrometric precision with which a pulsar timing array (PTA) can localize a single astrophysical gravitational-wave source, in the regime where pulsar distances are poorly constrained compared to the gravitational wavelength. Using simple matched-filter, map-making simulations, we calculate the astrometric precision of the intrinsic PTA residual response as a function of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where the SNR is that of the source in the matched-filter map, and find that the median angular error decreases as $\sqrt{\ln 2/3}\,/[\mathrm{SNR}\sqrt{\ln\mathrm{SNR}}]$ over the relevant SNR range, with a pre-factor we derive from first principles. At an SNR of 6, this log term coming from the singular core of the convolution kernel produces an angular error approximately $1.4$ times smaller than for a Gaussian beam. We compare this sky-averaged maximum precision with the precision achieved across the sky by the pulsars of the International Pulsar Timing Array (IPTA) DR2. For a map with SNR of 6, the intrinsic array precision is $3.3^\circ$. For the IPTA configuration at the same SNR, the median precision over the sky is worse due to sparse sampling of the underlying pulsar residual response, approximately $8.9^\circ$; however, for sources in $14\%$ of the sky, the high local pulsar density yields a precision better than $3.3^\circ$.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): The Euclid surveys at DR1
comment: Paper intended for the A&A Special Issue 'Euclid First data release'
summary: Euclid is a surveying mission that is progressively imaging and spectroscopically mapping a wide area of extragalactic sky in visible and near infrared bands. The Euclid mission is, however, not restricted to the Euclid Wide Survey, but it includes data from various other survey components. This paper presents the Data Release 1 (DR1) status of the multiple Euclid surveys and fields, including the Euclid Deep Survey, Euclid Auxiliary Fields, calibration fields, the Euclid Medium-Deep Survey, the Euclid Ecliptic Survey, and the Independent Legacy Scientists' field, in addition to the Euclid Wide Survey. Some of these fields were observed during the initial Performance-Verification phase, others during the Phase-Diversity calibration campaign, and the majority during the subsequent science operations phase. This paper describes the different procedures of survey implementation applied in the various phases of the mission, from the set of requirements, constraints, and limitations, to the final operational products used to operate the spacecraft and execute the science surveys. The resulting main component of the Euclid surveys, the Euclid Wide Survey, covers at DR1 an area of 2100$\,{\rm deg}^2$, in two separate regions, of which 1900$\,{\rm deg}^2$ corresponds to data validated in higher-level processing.

title: A Variable Compact Millimeter Excess in the Type-1 Seyfert Galaxy NGC 985: Implications for a Black-Hole Corona
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Compact millimeter emission from radio-quiet active galactic nuclei has been proposed as a probe of magnetized accretion-disk coronae. We present three epochs of ALMA observations of the type-1 Seyfert galaxy NGC 985, together with archival post-upgrade VLA data presented here for the first time, to investigate its compact millimeter excess. The millimeter flux density decreased strongly between the first two ALMA epochs separated by approximately one month, while the component was detected again at an intermediate level in the third epoch. This variability demonstrates an intrinsically variable compact component and implies a model-independent size limit of $\lesssim 0.024$ pc ($\simeq 1.1\times10^3 R_{\rm S}$). Spectral decomposition requires a compact, self-absorbed synchrotron component to reproduce the millimeter-wave data. A hybrid thermal/nonthermal coronal model reproduces the radio-millimeter spectra, with the two broadly sampled ALMA epochs favoring different nonthermal electron distributions. The estimated radiative cooling times are comparable to or shorter than the light-crossing time, implying continuous injection or reacceleration of nonthermal electrons; a change in particle injection is the most natural driver of the observed spectral changes. We conclude that NGC 985 hosts a recurrent and variable compact millimeter synchrotron component. A magnetized corona provides a plausible origin, although the present data do not uniquely distinguish a coronal origin from alternatives such as a jet base.

title: Modelling redshift-space distortions with tracer-centred split densities
comment: 20 pages, 18 figures
summary: Analysing galaxy clustering in split environmental densities has been demonstrated to offer an advantage over standard two-point clustering for extracting cosmological information. A major challenge to realising this potential with the density-split (DS) technique is that the observations are in redshift space. This complicates its modelling, primarily because the density-split centres may not be conserved between real and redshift space. We develop a modelling framework that splits on the tracer-centred density PDF, rather than the volume-weighted density PDF commonly used in previous studies. We derive the linear bias associated with the threshold density in redshift space, enabling us to connect large-scale DS clustering to the density PDF. We find that the threshold density field consists of doughnut-like structures, which we term `Island(s)'. We propose an empirical model, analogous to the halo model framework, that comprises linear, non-linear, and stochastic terms and accurately reproduces the anisotropic redshift-space clustering of tracers in each DS bin. Using this model, we confirm that DS clustering can provide tighter constraints on cosmological parameters than the standard two-point statistic. Furthermore, we show that the gain in cosmological information from DS analyses relative to standard two-point statistics arises primarily from knowledge of the density PDF, which incorporates small-scale perturbation modes below the smoothing scale.

title: A deterministic theory of kinetic fluctuations in long-range interacting homogeneous systems without collective effects
comment: 27 pages, 6 figures, submitted to APS
summary: Finite-$N$ fluctuations govern the slow relaxation of long-range interacting systems, yet accessing their full statistics demands huge ensembles of costly simulations. We show that, in homogeneous systems without collective effects, this statistical problem collapses onto just three deterministic kinetic equations. Starting from the Landau-Dean-Kawasaki equation, i.e. the stochastic counterpart of the large deviation principle for the Landau equation, we derive the infinite hierarchy of $n$-point moments of the empirical distribution function at leading order in $1/N$. We prove that it is solved exactly by a quasi-Gaussian closure. The resulting minimal Landau fluctuation hierarchy is formed by the Landau equation, a Lyapunov equation for the two-point moment, and a kinetic equation for the three-point moment. From these three equations, all higher-order moments follow algebraically. The hierarchy exactly preserves the collisional invariants and their fluctuations, and predicts the full probability distribution of observables in the central fluctuation regime. Benchmarked against $N$-body realizations, it reproduces the mean, variance and higher-order moments with an accuracy that improves systematically with $N$. A single deterministic time-integration of three coupled partial differential equations thus replaces large ensembles of simulations, for any large $N$.

title: Magellanic Outflow and Chemistry Survey (MAGOS): the Outflow-Luminosity Scaling Relations in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, accepted for publication in the ApJL
summary: Understanding massive star formation in low-metallicity environments is crucial for constraining the universality of star formation across cosmic evolution. In this Letter, we present the first systematic survey of massive protostellar outflows in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC, $Z\sim$0.2--0.5 $Z_\odot$), as part of the Magellanic Outflow and Chemistry Survey (MAGOS). MAGOS targets 40 massive young stellar objects (MYSOs) with luminosities of (1--23)$\times 10^4$ $L_\odot$ with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 0.85 mm at a linear resolution of $\sim$0.1 pc. Using CO (3--2), we identify blue- and red-shifted outflows associated with the primary continuum sources toward 29 targets in the LMC and 10 targets in the SMC. Comparing the outflow mass, momentum, energy, and force versus luminosity scaling relations in MAGOS with those in the Galaxy, we find that the LMC CO outflows have a similar slope in the mass-luminosity relation, suggesting that CO remains an effective tracer of massive protostellar outflows at $Z\sim$0.5 $Z_\odot$. In contrast, despite the large scatter, the SMC CO outflows are deficient at high luminosity and show flatter scaling relations than the LMC and the Galaxy. This is consistent with reduced CO abundances due to enhanced photodissociation at high luminosity and low metallicity ($Z\sim$0.2 $Z_\odot$), although the possibility of intrinsically weak outflow launching cannot be ruled out with the current data.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Multi-band photometry validation on COSMOS extragalactic sources
comment: Paper intended for the A\&A Special Issue "Euclid First Data Release''
summary: The Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) contains catalogues of sources covering 1900 deg2, including deep coverage of legacy fields that enable an extensive comparison between Euclid imaging and multiwavelength observations from other instruments. The Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field, observed by Euclid and included in DR1, has been observed with the James Webb Space Telescope, resulting in the COSMOS2025 catalogue. We compare the Euclid DR1 photometry with the multiwavelength COSMOS2025 data to assess the accuracy of the photometric measurements produced by the different methods implemented in the OU-MER pipeline. We use both the Euclid Wide and Deep Surveys, focussing exclusively on extragalactic sources. We use the fluxes of COSMOS2025 to predict the expected fluxes in the Euclid bands via spectral energy distribution fitting, while the redshifts are either spectroscopic, for a sample of brighter sources, or photometric, to include fainter sources. Both the fluxes in the common Hyper Suprime-Cam bands and the SEDs from COSMOS2025 are used to validate the analysis and to characterise any biases or limitations of the method. The predicted fluxes and the OU-MER measurements are in good agreement, especially for bright and isolated sources. Median offsets depend on band, photometric method, survey depth, and redshift sample, most well within 10%, the largest offset seen in the NIR bands for the deep photo-z model-fitting measurements. However, complementary measurements on Gaia stars show an opposite trend, highlighting that photometric validation approaches may suffer from intrinsic uncertainties that prevent a thorough assessment of systematic effects. Among the three methods, template-fitting photometry generally shows the smallest offset from the SED-based predictions in the NISP bands and toward fainter magnitudes, while aperture photometry and model-fitting are comparable in IE.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) Euclid photometric masks
summary: This paper describes the Euclid DR1 photometric masks, which trace spatial variations in the survey properties (e.g. satellite position angles, integration time, sky tiling, and survey footprint); in the instrumental performance of Euclid and the external data (EXT) it uses (e.g. survey coverage, depth, PSF width, quality flags, systematic effects and astrometric uncertainties); and in possible contamination from sky emission (e.g. galactic extinction and zodiacal light emission). Among this, the effective coverage mask is particularly important as it defines the effective survey area and can be used to exclude spurious objects when selecting Euclid photometric samples for scientific analyses. The Euclid photometric masks are built for each observed sky region (tile) and are provided as full-sky HEALPix maps (nested ordering and explicit indexing) at Nside = 16 384, equating to a resolution of 12"88, for both the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and Euclid Deep Survey (EDS). We estimate the total area of the DR1 EWS (EDS) to be 2008.8 (74.7) deg$^2$ and find that 82 (81)\% of this area is preserved by the effective coverage mask. We observe that Euclid's instrumental properties are consistent with expectations, showing only minor relative variations across the sky. For DR1 EWS the standard deviation of the depth (computed for a 2" aperture and at 5 $σ$) is below 0.2 AB mag, with median values of 25.69, 24.14, 24.3, and 24.29 for the Euclid IE, YE, JE, and HE bands. Finally, we expect these photometric masks to be key to many science applications and in particular for cosmological analyses.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): Calibration strategy and observations
comment: 43 pages, 17 figures; companion paper of Euclid DR1
summary: This paper reviews how Euclid's top-level calibration requirements were translated into a calibration plan, how this plan is implemented and maintained during the survey, and how it performs in the current DR1 release. We show that DR1 already meets or exceeds most end-of-mission spectrophotometric calibration requirements. The construction of spectroscopically complete and pure samples relies on ongoing data acquisition for the Euclid Deep Survey, while point-spread-function modelling and shear calibration are still converging to their stringent accuracy requirements. With all DR1 data reprocessed with the DR1 pipeline configuration, more subtle effects have been detected and characterised, and correction strategies have been developed for DR2. These include improved absolute flux calibration, astrometry, charge-persistence correction, shutter effects, wavelength calibration, and spectrophotometric corrections for water-ice contamination. Finally, synthetic photometric transformations between Euclid and each of Roman, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope, are presented.

title: Euclid First Data Release 1 (DR1) - Data release overview
comment: Paper intended for the A\&A Special Issue 'Euclid First Data Release'. 11 pages, 4 figures
summary: This paper describes the contents of the Euclid First Data Release (DR1), together with the set of papers that document the data-processing and the data products. DR1 consists of two parts: first `DR1-Foundation', releasing images, spectra, and catalogues in November 2026. Second, the shear measurements and the `Level~3' products required for cosmological analyses will be added in June 2027 to complete the full DR1. This data set contains around a billion catalogued objects, mainly from the Euclid Wide Survey (1975\,deg$^2$) and the Euclid Deep Fields (77\,deg$^2$)

title: Euclid: Data Release 1 (DR1) - First NISP emission-line maps: Methodology, validation, and applications to galaxy evolution
comment: Paper intended for the A&A Special Issue "Euclid First Data Release''. 18 pages, 15 figures
summary: We demonstrate the capability of the slitless spectroscopic mode of the Euclid Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) to produce emission-line maps analogous to narrow-band images with user-defined central wavelengths. We present the first such maps of galaxies at $0.4 < z < 0.9$, constructed from blue-grism exposures obtained during the Euclid performance-verification observations of the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field in November 2023. We demonstrate the use of these maps for identifying star-forming clumps, measuring radial star-formation profiles, detecting projected internal velocity gradients, deblending the H$α$--[N II] complex, and assessing spectroscopic redshift measurements. As a first statistical application, we reconstruct the galaxy mass--metallicity relation for 885 galaxies observed with the blue grism at $0.4 < z < 0.9$ by deblending the H$α$--[N II] complex in the emission-line maps, and measure stacked H$α$ radial profiles for 2634 galaxies over the same redshift range. The mass--metallicity relation is consistent with that obtained from the Euclid 1D spectroscopic measurements, demonstrating overall agreement between the two deblending approaches. The recovered H$α$ radial profiles broadly follow the $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ stellar continuum but remain modestly more extended after matching the $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ images to the H$α$ PSF, consistent with previous results in the literature. Across the four $Y_{\mathrm{E}}$ size bins, we measure a mean $R_{50,\mathrm{H}α}/R_{50,Y_{\mathrm{E}}}=1.15$.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). NIR astrometric calibration
comment: Paper intended for the A&A Special Issue "Euclid First Data Release''(12 pages, 12 figures)
summary: This paper presents the methodology and results of the astrometric calibration applied to the Euclid Near-Infrared (NIR) images in the Euclid Data Release 1, focusing on the techniques used to model and correct instrumental distortions, as well as the assessment of calibration quality. This work details the calibration pipeline, including quality control tests, and the evaluation of astrometric residuals against the Gaia DR3 catalogue and internal consistency metrics based on data encompassing more than one year of Euclid operation: the achieved accuracy is 30 mas for 97% of the total area, thus exceeding the requirements for Data Release 1. For the remaining 3%, accuracy declines due to a persistence correction issue: a method to correct the issue is presented. Furthermore, we discuss the stability of the solution over time, its dependence on source properties and instrument configuration, and outline the improvements planned for future Euclid data releases to enhance the astrometric calibration accuracy and efficiency.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). The PHZ processing function for the physical properties of galaxies
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures. Paper intended for the A\&A Special Issue "Euclid First Data Release''
summary: Euclid is a European Space Agency mission mapping the extragalactic sky, aiming to provide the most-accurate 3D view of the Universe at optical and near-infrared wavelengths, by measuring the photometric redshifts of billions of galaxies. Within the Euclid Consortium, this task is executed by the PHZ Organisation Unit. PHZ takes as input the multi-wavelength photometry of Euclid and ground-based data, and returns as output the source classification, photometric redshifts for the Euclid core science (i.e., cosmology), and photometric redshifts plus physical parameters and absolute magnitudes for non-cosmological science. As part of the first Euclid Data Release (DR1), we describe the details of the DR1 pipeline for non-cosmological science, along with the released data products, and their validation. The non-cosmological science data products are obtained with NNPZ, a nearest-neighbour algorithm developed within PHZ that infers the properties of each target galaxy from its closest matches, in colour-magnitude space, within a reference sample of galaxies with known redshifts and physical parameters. We built this reference sample from Euclid observations of COSMOS, one of the Euclid Auxiliary Fields, labelling each galaxy with redshifts and physical parameters derived from the COSMOS2020 multi-wavelength photometry, consistently with the Euclid core-science results. Combined with the adjustments and priors required to generalise the results across the entire extragalactic sky, this approach yields high-quality and internally consistent data products. We tested the performance using both internal metrics and comparisons to ancillary data sets (e.g., COSMOS2020, 3D-HST, and DESI) and scaling relations (e.g., the star-forming main sequence); the results are in line with expectations and pre-DR1 simulations for both the Euclid Wide Survey and Euclid Deep Fields.

title: Galaxy Clustering Topology in Observations and Cosmological Simulations
comment: 11 pages,6 figures,3 tables
summary: We present a genus topology analysis of the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data (SDSS), comparing the observed topology with mock galaxy samples from the Horizon Run 4 (HR4) $N$-body simulation and four cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. We construct nine volume-limited samples and measure their genus curves at Gaussian smoothing scales of $4$--$12~h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$. Overall, the modern galaxy models reproduce the observed genus statistics substantially better than the HGC, HOD, and SAM models examined by Choi et al. (2010). Among the models considered here, the HR4 Most-Bound-Halo Particle galaxy-assignment model shows somewhat better overall agreement with the SDSS topology than IllustrisTNG300 and FLAMINGO. The observed scale dependences of the genus shift parameter $Δν_f$ and void abundance parameter $A_V$ are somewhat steeper than those predicted by the simulations, but their joint discrepancy from HR4 is not statistically significant. The smaller-volume TNG100 and EAGLE realizations show significant excesses in $A_C$, at $4.5σ$ and $7.0σ$, respectively, relative to the observational uncertainties. When the expected cosmic variance of the simulations is taken into account, they do not necessarily indicate failures of the galaxy-formation prescriptions, but they caution that individual small-volume realizations may not be representative of the observed galaxy topology. Overall, modern galaxy formation models reproduce the observed topology substantially better than earlier models, while residual differences remain that can be tested more precisely with denser future surveys.

title: 3D radiative transfer of K-series lines of He-like ions with SKIRT
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: High-resolution X-ray spectroscopy with XRISM has resolved line profiles of highly ionised ions, including P Cygni profiles, in many systems containing compact objects. To interpret these line profiles, forward modelling with three-dimensional radiative transfer (3D RT) calculations including the relevant ionic processes is required. Following our previous work on the Lyman-series lines of H-like ions, we present the implementation of the K-series lines of He-like ions with Z = 2-30 in the open-source Monte Carlo RT code SKIRT, providing a numerical tool for interpreting highresolution X-ray spectra of photoionised plasmas. Building upon the framework developed for H-like ions, we incorporate the resonance scattering (RS) and radiative recombination (RR) channels. We also implement the inner-shell ionisation (II) channel of Li-like ions for the production of He-like lines. We resolve fine-structure levels and account for level populations, frequency redistribution, phase function, and linear polarisation through transition-specific Mueller matrices. The implementation reproduces the expected RT effects in He-like lines. The Fe xxv w and y lines, dominated by the RS channel, develop optically thick line-profile distortions and P Cygni profiles in an outflowing plasma, whereas the x and z lines, dominated by the RR and II channels, do not exhibit such behaviour. The line intensities from the RS and RR channels agree well with Cloudy. The II channel further enhances the z line, which is not yet included in Cloudy. The linear polarisation calculations reproduce the analytical and experimental angular dependence of resonance scattering on a line-by-line basis. This extension to He-like lines, together with our previous implementation of H-like lines, enables 3D RT modelling of the major X-ray lines, providing a tool for constraining gas kinematics around compact objects observed with XRISM.

title: Machine-Learning Reconstruction of Intergalactic Medium Column-Density Maps from Observed Ly$α$ Emission Cubes
comment: 35 pages, 20 figures. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ)
summary: Understanding the large-scale structure of the intergalactic medium (IGM) is essential for studying galaxy evolution, particularly at $z \sim 2$--$6$, when cold filaments in the cosmic web are considered a primary mechanism for fueling galaxy growth. At these redshifts, Ly$α$ emission shifts into the optical regime and serves as the primary tracer of diffuse IGM for ground-based integral field units (IFUs). However, detections remain limited by low signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) and the complexities of resonant scattering. We present a proof-of-concept machine-learning framework to reconstruct IGM gas column-density maps from noisy Ly$α$ IFU emission cubes. Using Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI) observations of $z \sim 2.3$ protoclusters as a case study, we train a custom convolutional neural network (CNN), the Column Density Estimator (CDE), on a simulated dataset combining IllustrisTNG100 with simplified radiative-transfer calculations and an approximate treatment of KCWI noise. The CDE successfully reconstructs broad filamentary structures in the simulated test set under these adopted assumptions. Applied to observed KCWI data, the CDE predicts gas column-density maps containing filamentary structures extending over $\gtrsim 40''$ ($\sim 1$ comoving Mpc), consistent with an IGM interpretation. The observed reconstructions remain conditional on the adopted models. These results illustrate the potential of the CDE framework for connecting diffuse Ly$α$ observations with simulations of the IGM.

title: The ZTF Variability Archive (ZVAR): Initial Data Release (DR1)
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, submitted to PASP, data is available at https://zvar.caltech.edu
summary: The Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) has observed the northern sky observable from Palomar Observatory since March 2018, accumulating a median of a thousand photometric measurements across $gri$ for each of more than a billion sources. Among these billions of objects are millions of periodically variable stars, active galactic nuclei, stellar remnants, and substellar objects. We describe the initial data release (DR1) of the ZTF Variability Archive (ZVAR) which provides image difference forced photometry, candidate periods, and variability metrics for approximately 1.3 billion sources in ZTF having an identification in Pan-STARRS1 DR1 (PS1). The data cover the 5.37 year interval between March 2018 and July 2023. ZVAR is sensitive to periods between 5 minutes and 2.7 years. We also describe tools for accessing the ZVAR data.

title: Globular Clusters in the Time of JWST. II. Looks like the second, moves like the first: the syrphid-like intermediate population of NGC 2808
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: The present-day kinematics of multiple populations in globular clusters can retain information about their initial conditions and can therefore help trace how the different populations formed. We combine JWST and HST photometry and proper motions to study the internal dynamics of four populations in NGC 2808 out to about eight half-light radii: the first population (1P) and three second-population groups with increasing light-element processing (2Pa, 2Pb, and 2Pc), providing the first detailed kinematic characterisation of the chemically intermediate 2Pa. We find significant kinematic differences between the populations. While all four have similar sky-projected radial velocity dispersions, 2Pb and 2Pc have lower tangential dispersions than 1P and are strongly radially anisotropic, whereas 2Pa shares the only mildly anisotropic kinematics of 1P. Therefore, chemically distinct 2P groups have different dynamical properties, suggesting that they formed under different conditions and/or experienced a different subsequent dynamical evolution. In the outer JWST field, the velocity dispersion depends only weakly on stellar mass, with hints of inverted equipartition. The difference between radial and tangential equipartition is similar for 1P and 2Pa and decreases towards 2Pc, a trend that remains tentative given the uncertainties. Our results show that 2P is not a dynamically homogeneous group, and that the kinematics of its individual groups provide a key constraint for multiple population formation scenarios.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Near-infrared processing and data products
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: The Euclid near-infrared processing function (NIR PF) converts the raw observations acquired by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) into calibrated images and source-level products. Following the first implementation delivered with the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1), the NIR PF has been revised for the first major Euclid Data Release (DR1), with improvements to detector-level processing, calibration, image reconstruction, and quality control. The DR1 processing includes observations covering more than $1900\,\rm{deg}^2$ and has produced $71\,659$ calibrated near-infrared (NIR) images. We assess the performance of the processing chain through extensive astrometric and photometric validation. The astrometric solution reaches an average root-mean-square (RMS) of 10 mas, remaining below 20 mas for 99% of the dithers in all three NISP bands. Temporal variations in the instrumental throughput are typically corrected to a level of 2 mmag RMS, while the relative photometric accuracy reaches 0.9% for sources brighter than 19 mag in $Y_\mathrm{E}$, $J_\mathrm{E}$, and $H_\mathrm{E}$, and the residual spatial variations of the photometric calibration across the focal plane are at the level of approximately 10 mmag for the entire sample. Despite some remaining limitations, the DR1 NIR imaging products are consistent with the required astrometric and photometric performance over the large area covered by this release.

title: Euclid: Data Release 1 (DR1) -- Bayesian 3D shape inference of star-forming galaxy populations
comment: Paper intended for the A&A Special Issue "Euclid First Data Release'', Submitted to A&A, 31 pages, 33 figures
summary: Understanding the intrinsic 3D shapes of galaxies provides crucial insights into their formation and evolution, but determining these from projections remains challenging. We apply a Bayesian inference framework to optical images of galaxies from the Euclid Data Release 1, leveraging its large sample size to test the scalability and robustness of this methodology. Applying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling to Sérsic axis ratios and effective radii, we constrain the population-level mean 3D ellipticity, triaxiality, and size, together with their covariances for $40\,864\,304$ star-forming galaxies with stellar masses $M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{10.5}M_\odot$ at redshifts $0<z<1.2$. Our sample size exceeds previous shape inference studies by factors of $440$--$52\,800$ relative to early observations by JWST, and factors of $440$--$17\,600$ relative to legacy observations from HST in overlapping mass-redshift bins, enabling finer binning alongside improved statistical constraints on shape evolution. We additionally include over 9 million galaxies at $z<0.5$, a regime historically limited by sample size in previous shape inference studies. We recover key evolutionary trends identified in previous smaller-sample studies. We find high ellipticities ($μ_E \sim 0.600$--$0.821$) across all bins, indicating that the underlying 3D shape distributions are statistically dominated by flattened geometries. Most notably, we recover the decline of the prolate fraction towards $z=0$ at low masses ($M_\ast=10^{9}$--$10^{9.5}M_\odot$) reported by previous studies. This trend is seen consistently in comparable analyses of independent data sets spanning different depths and resolution regimes, showing that it is not an artefact of small-sample statistics, suggesting it may be a genuine feature of galaxy evolution. We also identify future methodological improvements for subsequent Euclid data releases.

title: Silent Heavy Fields: An Exclusion Rule for the Cosmological Collider
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, plus appendix
summary: The cosmological collider uses oscillatory signatures in primordial correlators to probe heavy fields during inflation. This probe has blind spots, as heavy fields can keep ticking in time while remaining silent in the correlators. In this letter, we derive an exclusion rule under which cosmological collider signals vanish. The rule covers two classes of diagrams where a de Sitter invariant heavy sector couples covariantly to a single external field at one vertex. We first prove it for exchanges mediated by the two-point function of the heavy sector to all loop orders, using a spectral decomposition followed by a field redefinition. The result then extends to one-loop polygons by matching their oscillatory contributions onto those of the first class. The approximate signals of previously studied processes that fall into these classes must therefore be revisited. As a nonvanishing example, we derive the leading signal of a triangle loop for the first time in a toy model motivated by chemical potentials.

title: Shear, vorticity, and $f(R)$ theories
comment: 23 pages, 9 figures. Published in Phys. Rev. D
summary: We study how an extended spherical collapse model (ESCM), including shear, vorticity and chameleon screening, modifies the collapse threshold $δ_c(z)$ and $δ_c(M)$, the turnaround density $δ_t$, the turnaround radius $R_t$ and the halo mass function in the Hu-Sawicki $f(R)$ model, and whether these quantities can distinguish $f(R)$ from General Relativity (GR). Unlike the standard spherical collapse model (SSCM), in the ESCM $δ_c$ depends on mass, redshift and $|f_{R0}|$; we use it to compute the halo mass function with the excursion set approach. Between GR and the large-field (LF) limit of $f(R)$, $δ_c$ differs by a few percent within the ESCM and by about 20% between GR in the ESCM and the LF limit in the SSCM; $δ_t$ differs by about 27-29% and $R_t$ by about 6.5%. With screening, the difference between GR and screened $δ_c$ is 2.5% for $|f_{R0}|=10^{-4}$ (F4) and vanishes for $|f_{R0}|=10^{-6}$ (F6); for $δ_t$ it is larger than 20% (F4), about 10% (F5) and 0 (F6); for $R_t$ about 6.5% (F4), 3% (F5) and 0 (F6). Since observations exclude F4 and F6 is practically identical to GR, only F5 could discriminate, but the ~20% uncertainty on measured turnaround radii rules out $R_t$ and related quantities as tests of $f(R)$. The halo abundance predicted by $f(R)$, especially at high redshift, can instead distinguish $f(R)$ from GR.

title: Where Do Population~III Stars Form? Unveiling Late PopIII-Forming Environments with CampFIRE-6k
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to RNAAS
summary: Population III (PopIII) stars are the first generation of metal-free stars, thought to form in minihalos ($M_\mathrm{halo} \sim10^5-10^6\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$) at Cosmic Dawn ($z\gtrsim15$) before largely giving way to Population II stars formed from the newly enriched medium. Simulations show, however, that PopIII stars may continue forming at low rates through the Epoch of Reionization (EoR, $z \sim 6 - 10$), due to the inhomogeneous enrichment of the Universe. Nonetheless, significant uncertainty remains on the rates and typical environments of late PopIII formation. We use the CampFIRE-6k cosmological zoom-in simulation to examine PopIII star formation history and environments through $z\sim6$. We find that PopIII stars form at a near constant rate ($\sim 10^{-3.5} ~\mathrm{M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}\,cMpc ^{-3}}$) through $z=6$, including within atomic-cooling halos ($M_\mathrm{halo}\sim 10^7-10^8\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$) at late times.

title: FastBox: A lightweight Python package for rapid cosmological 21cm intensity mapping simulations
comment: Prepared for submission to JOSS
summary: FastBox is a Python package for generating fast, physically realistic simulations of cosmological signals in three-dimensional co-moving boxes, with the primary focus of its application being 21cm intensity mapping (IM) experiments. It provides a framework for producing cosmology-dependent Gaussian and log-normal density fields, as well as modelling the effects of redshift-space distortions and linear biasing, among others. Models of instrumental systematics are incorporated, including radiometer noise and beam convolutions. Diffuse and point source foreground models are included, along with a number of foreground filtering strategies such as PCA, ICA, and transfer function correction via mock signal injection. Lastly, estimators are provided for power spectra, the two-point correlation function, and the equilateral bispectrum. The same underlying density field can also be Poisson-sampled into a discrete galaxy catalogue, so that 21cm and galaxy tracers are simulated from common initial conditions and their cross-power spectrum can be measured. Simulation grids may be cubic or anisotropic, with independent side lengths and cell counts along each Cartesian axis. FastBox is designed as a lightweight but realistic test-bench for the development and validation of end-to-end cosmological analysis pipelines.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): VIS processing and data products
comment: Paper intended for the A&A Special Issue "Euclid First Data Release''
summary: This paper describes the characteristics of the Euclid visible imager (VIS) data delivered as part of the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). This data set contains 42092 calibrated frames. Validated nominal exposures cover 2092 deg$^2$ of sky. We outline the minor changes made to the VIS processing function (PF) since previous releases. For the wide survey, the photometric and astrometric accuracy of the reference stellar sample $(18.5 < I_{\rm E} < 19.8)$ is excellent. The internal and external astrometric dispersions are 0.08 and 0.18 mas, respectively, at the quadrant level, and 3.4 and 5.6 mas at the source level. The corresponding internal and external photometric dispersions are 0.76 and 1.4 mmag at the quadrant level, and 11 and 25 mmag at the source level. We characterise remaining astrometric and photometric systematic effects: focal-plane-dependent variations; time-dependent photometric offsets; and colour-dependent centroid shifts. The noise floor in the deepest VIS images appears to be set by the extended diffuse light of faint galaxies. Globally, the DR1 VIS data meet pre-launch mission requirements and the 42092 images it contains provide our first substantial look at the sky as seen by VIS.

title: Cubic Curvature Deformations to the Kerr Black Hole Shadow
comment: 28 pages, 11 figures
summary: We investigate the effects of cubic curvature corrections on the shadows of rotating black holes within the effective field theory of gravity. Starting from a perturbatively corrected Kerr metric incorporating two independent cubic curvature couplings, we construct black hole shadows through numerical integration of null geodesics, without assuming separability of the geodesic equations. Using a Hamiltonian ray-tracing approach, we systematically examine the dependence of the shadow geometry on the higher-curvature couplings, black hole spin, and observer inclination. We find that cubic curvature interactions can produce discernible deviations from the Kerr shadow, modifying its apparent size and shape. In particular, the two cubic interactions exhibit distinct effects on the shadow boundary, with the magnitude of the deviations depending sensitively on the coupling strengths and black hole spin. We validate our numerical results through independent convergence tests of the geodesic integration and shadow-boundary determination, and recover the analytical Kerr shadow in the vanishing-coupling limit. Our results provide a complementary probe of higher-curvature gravity in the strong-field regime and illustrate the potential of black hole shadow observations to constrain departures from general relativity.

title: Exploring a Correlation Between AGN Black Hole Mass and X-ray Luminosity
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure
summary: The traditional method to measure Type-1 Active Galactic Nuclei central black hole masses ($M_{BH}$) is the reverberation mapping (RM) technique. Motivated by the desire to find a less observationally expensive method (than RM) to estimate $M_{BH}$, we have explored a purported correlation between X-ray luminosity and $M_{BH}$. For this we have compiled a sample of 35 AGN with RM $M_{BH}$ estimates that were detected in the eROSITA All-Sky Survey public data release. Using a sample that is larger than that of J. A. Mayers et al. 2018 and has a cleaner selection function, we confirm their XMM-Newton based result of a positive correlation. However, the scatter on the scaling relation remains too high ($σ_\mathrm{int}=0.50^{+0.08}_{-0.06}$) to make this a practical method to predict $M_{BH}$ for a given X-ray detected Type-1 AGN. That said, our findings can be used to improve mock X-ray skies generated from large volume hydrodynamical cosmological simulations. Such mocks are a necessary ingredient for cluster cosmology and preparation for future missions such as NewAthena.

title: Euclid DR1 Legacy Science on Ultracool Dwarfs: Brown Dwarfs in the Blanco 1 Open Cluster
comment: 59 pages, 23 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: A 35.6\,deg$^2$ field of Euclid Data Release~1 that covers part of the corona and tidal tails of the young (100--130\,Myr) nearby (234\,pc) open cluster Blanco~1 is presented. We select 22 ultracool dwarfs from Euclid photometry and slitless spectra, and measure proper motions over a median baseline of 13\,yr by combining Euclid astrometry with VIKING, KiDS and Rubin positions. Ten objects are comoving late-M and L dwarf candidates with membership probabilities of at least 0.5 under two field models. Nine of them are typed from their Euclid spectra, and the tenth is a candidate only if its colour-based type is adopted. Brown dwarf evolutionary models give masses of 0.03--0.06\,$M_\odot$ for the cluster age. The substellar population is about twice that predicted by a lognormal mass function scaled to the cluster's Gaia members. The remaining 12 objects are classified as late-M, L and T dwarfs with low probability of membership in the cluster. Using the Euclid sample to calibrate a search over 246\,deg$^2$ of VIKING and KiDS photometry and motions, we identify 60 ultracool candidates, with about seven expected by chance. In the core region of Blanco 1 archival Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam images and motions over 2011--2025 yield 35 candidates of types M7 or later, at least 20 of which are kinematic members at 95\% confidence. These results extend the spectroscopic sequence of Blanco 1 into the L-type brown dwarfs and the list of candidate members over the outskirts and tidal tails of the cluster.

title: Triple-Massive-Exchange Bispectrum of Quasi-Single-Field Inflation
comment: 9 pages
summary: The triple-exchange bispectrum of the scalar quasi-single-field inflation model has resisted analytic evaluation across its full parameter space since its advent, despite rapid progress in cosmological collider physics.
